name: virel
author: toys-and-building agent
description: Toy block wall, v3 (one-course pass; v2 kept as virel.v2.json, v1 as virel.v1.json). v2 was too_hard (4 Opus finals at 14/16/0/2 %, three of them WITH a demo): players learned the format from the demo but building a WHOLE WALL of >=5 courses carrying exactly N twin stacks was a search they never finished, so identical answers scored 1 with one clue and 0 with another. v3 keeps the counted relation and collapses the construction to ONE course. CLUE = a finished wall, drawn top course first, one line per course, 3-4 courses, each a gapless tiling of the same width W in 14..20 by bricks 2-6 wide (`[]`=2 ... `[----]`=6), then a last line with N in 0..3. ANSWER = the same wall with ONE MORE COURSE on top: line 1 is the new course (a gapless tiling of the same width, bricks 2-6), lines 2.. are the clue's wall unchanged, and the new course makes exactly N TWIN STACKS with the course below it. A twin = a brick sitting exactly on a brick of the same span (same left AND right edge). One clause a kid says in a breath: 'add one row so that exactly N bricks sit right on top of a brick the same size.' The scorer accepts the clue's trailing parameter line kept or dropped (house rule 2026-09-05). N is drawn 0:15 / 1:30 / 2:35 / 3:20 %; the width budget makes N and W correlated (N>=1 needs W>=16, N=2 W>=18, N=3 W=20-ish) which leaks nothing, since N is in the clue. FOOTHOLD (measured, 500 fresh clues): a demo-less player reads 'a wall and a number - send the wall with a row on top' straight off the clue; a random gapless course on top scores 15-23 % (15.4 % with 4-6 bricks, 22.4 % uniform over all tilings, 22.6 % with 5-7), and on the ~15 % of clues with N=0 any twin-free course scores, so a plain running bond scores 12.2 % on its own. Stacking the clue's top course again scores 0 % by arithmetic (the clue's courses have 4-8 bricks, so that is 4-8 twins and N<=3); the clue returned unchanged, junk, constants and demo replay all score 0-3 %. Best rival families: 'N joints line up' 31.2 %, 'N bricks centred on a wider brick' 27.1 %, 'a fixed brick count' 26.4 %, 'N same-width bricks in the course' 23.4 %, 'N bricks the same width as some brick below' 19.5 %, 'N bricks sharing exactly one edge' 12.5 %. No template exceeds ~31 %; the rule scores 100 %. DEMOS: generate() builds the clue's top course and a witness new course together out of a library of 463 two-row gadgets, so every shipped demo can show, in the SAME picture: the N twins (the widest >=3 wide, >=4 on about half the clues), >=1 brick CENTRED on a wider brick below (equal overhang both sides - kills 'sits inside'), >=1 brick of the SAME WIDTH as one below but offset by exactly one column (kills 'same size'), and a joint that lines up without a twin under it on ~79 % of clues. Every count that could be mistaken for N - bricks in the new course, joints that line up, pairs sharing exactly one edge, courses - is forced to differ from N, and the clue's own junctions all carry a twin count != N (and >=1 at the top junction) so 'count the twins in the whole wall' and 'copy a course up' both fail. Residual ambiguity, deliberate: the new course has exactly one centred brick and one offset brick, so on N=1 clues (30 %) the demo alone does not separate 'twins' from 'centred' from 'same width shifted'; one round of probes does, and each rival tops out at ~27 %. solve() enumerates every tiling of the width, keeps those that satisfy the rule and the demo constraints (median 2 candidates) and picks among them with random.Random(clue).

def score(c,s):
 R=[r for r in s.split()if not r.isdigit()];c=c.split()
 if len(R)!=len(c)or R[1:]!=c[:-1]:return 0
 b=re.findall(r"\[-{0,4}\]",R[0])
 if "".join(b)!=R[0]:return 0
 A=[];x=0
 for t in b:x+=len(t);A+=[(x-len(t),x)]
 B=[];y=0
 for t in re.findall(r"\[-*\]",R[1]):y+=len(t);B+=[(y-len(t),y)]
 return int(x==y and len(set(A)&set(B))==int(c[-1]))
